stories.title: The Mending Room
passages: The notice appeared on the break-room corkboard on a Tuesday, taped over last month's shift schedule, and by noon everyone on the floor had read it twice. Millbrook Garment would close its doors in three weeks. Nora Vance stood at her station with a half-finished collar still pinned beneath the presser foot, listening to the hum of thirty machines fall silent one by one as women switched them off and started to cry, or curse, or simply stare. She had given this floor fifteen years, long enough to know the particular ache of the chair, the trick to keeping bobbin thread from snarling in July's humidity, and none of it mattered now. On the drive home she pulled over twice, unable to see the road through her own tears. Her daughter Mia was eight and needed new sneakers before the school year started. There was three hundred and forty dollars in the checking account and rent was six hundred and ten. Nora sat in the parked car outside their apartment for a long time before going in, trying to compose a face that would not frighten her daughter, failing, and going in anyway.

Three weeks became six, and six became a winter Nora had not budgeted for. The unemployment checks were smaller than she had calculated and slower than the bills that kept arriving. By January the landlord had taped a five-day notice to her door, the paper curling in the cold, and Nora had already sold the television and her mother's ring before she let herself consider the sewing machine, the good one, the industrial machine she had bought used with her first bonus a decade ago. She sat with it in her lap the night before the pawnshop opened, running her thumb along the cold metal wheel, thinking about all the hems and zippers and quiet held-together mornings it had given her family. Mia asked why the machine was not in its corner anymore, and Nora told her it was being fixed, then locked herself in the bathroom and let the water run so her daughter would not hear her cry. She had stopped answering calls from numbers she did not recognize. She had stopped, most days, believing that any of it would turn around. There did not seem to be a future she could see clearly enough to walk toward.

The cleaning job came through a flyer stapled to a telephone pole, and Nora took it without asking what it paid, because asking felt like a luxury. Four houses a day, three days a week, scrubbing other families' grout and folding other families' laundry while Mia stayed with a neighbor for a few dollars an hour Nora could barely spare. Her knees ached in a new way each evening. One client, a brisk woman named Mrs. Calder, corrected her twice about how the throw pillows should be arranged and left no tip, and Nora said thank you anyway, because there were more houses on that street and she needed the reference. On the bus home she counted the bills twice, folded them into her sock the way her own mother used to, and did the math against the electric bill for the third time that day, hoping it would come out differently. It never did, not by much. Some nights she took in a neighbor's torn coat or a split seam for five dollars cash, working at the kitchen table after Mia was asleep, and told herself it was not a job, just a favor, because calling it a job made the smallness of it too real to bear.

The car's transmission gave out on a Thursday, coughing to a stop two blocks from the Calders' house, and Nora walked the rest of the way in the rain because being late meant being replaced. That night Mia woke with a fever that climbed past a hundred and two, and Nora sat on the edge of the bathtub doing arithmetic she hated, the co-pay against the grocery money against the bus fare she would need all week now that the car was dead. She chose the urgent care clinic and ate crackers for dinner instead of a proper meal, telling Mia it was a special treat, breakfast for dinner, and her daughter believed her because she was eight and had no reason yet not to. The doctor said it was only a virus. Nora cried in the parking lot from relief and then, almost immediately, from the newer worry of the bill that would arrive in six weeks. She picked up two more mending jobs that week from a bulletin board at the laundromat, hemming a stranger's curtains at midnight with the machine borrowed back temporarily from the pawnshop, paying interest on her own scissors, in a manner of speaking, just to finish the work.

A woman named Denise found Nora's number pinned beside the laundromat's lost-and-found board and asked her to alter eleven bridesmaid dresses before a wedding in nine days. It was more work than Nora had taken on since the factory closed, and she said yes before naming a price, then spent three nights hunched over the borrowed machine, her shoulders locked with tension, taking in seams and letting out others by lamplight after Mia went to bed. When the dresses were finished, pressed, and hung in garment bags on Denise's porch railing, Denise answered the door in a bathrobe, thanked her too quickly, and said she would send the money that weekend. The weekend passed. So did the following one. Nora sent two polite texts and then a third, less polite, and received nothing back at all. She thought about small claims court and then thought about the filing fee she did not have. The rent was due in four days and she was two hundred and sixty dollars short, a number she now knew the way she knew her own daughter's birthday, and she sat at the kitchen table doing the math yet again, as if repetition might change the total.

By spring, Nora had a standing arrangement with Ferraro's Dry Cleaning, mending and altering whatever the counter clerk set aside for her twice a week: a stuck zipper, a boy's school pants let down at the hem, a suit jacket needing new buttons. It was not much, but it was regular, and regular had come to feel like its own kind of luxury. She picked up the bundle on Tuesdays and Fridays, worked through it at her kitchen table while the radio played, and dropped the finished pieces back before the shop closed. The pay covered rent and groceries most months, with a little left for Mia's shoes, which no longer had cardboard wedged into split soles. Ferraro himself, an older man with reading glasses pushed up on his forehead, had started calling her the good one to customers who asked who had fixed their coat so well. Nora did not love the work, exactly, but she no longer dreaded Tuesdays. She had stopped checking the mail with her stomach in a knot. Some evenings she and Mia watched television together on the secondhand couch without either of them mentioning money at all, which felt, these days, like an accomplishment worth noting quietly to herself.

Nora added a shelf of thread spools to the kitchen wall that spring, organized by color the way she used to keep her station at the factory, and found she liked looking at it more than she expected to. Business stayed steady without growing much. She lost a week of income when Mia caught the flu going around her school, then made most of it back mending a batch of choir robes for the church two streets over, a job Ferraro had passed her way without being asked to. She still counted every dollar. She still drove the new-used car carefully, aware it was one bad repair from becoming another Thursday like the last one. But she had started keeping a coffee can of loose change behind the flour, a small buffer against the next surprise, and twice that month she had not needed to touch it. A woman from two buildings over asked if Nora could take in a wedding dress for her niece, and Nora quoted a fair price without apologizing for it, which was new. Nothing about her life looked remarkable from the outside. From the inside, it had stopped being an emergency, which was its own kind of relief.

The choir robes led, in a roundabout way, to a woman named Priscilla Odom, who ran a small boutique downtown and had seen one of the altered robes on her nephew. Priscilla came by Ferraro's counter asking who had done the work and left with Nora's phone number written on a receipt. She called two days later with an odd request: could Nora rework a vintage coat, taking it apart almost entirely and rebuilding the shoulders and lining to Priscilla's sketch, for a client willing to pay well if it turned out right. Nora said yes and then spent that night staring at the sketch, unsure whether she had the skill for garment construction rather than repair; it was one thing to fix a hem, another to build a shoulder from nothing. She said none of that doubt to Priscilla. She bought a secondhand dress form with money from the coffee can and set it up in the corner of the bedroom, where it stood for two days like a question she had not answered yet. Mia thought the headless, armless form was funny and then, after a week of watching her mother work on it every night, stopped laughing and started watching more carefully.

The coat came out better than Nora had let herself hope, the shoulders sitting clean and the lining falling the way Priscilla had drawn it, and the client who had commissioned it wore it to a gallery opening and was stopped twice to ask who had made it. Priscilla called before the weekend was over with two more requests and a suggestion Nora had not considered: a small consignment rack at the front of the boutique for pieces Nora reworked herself, sold under her own name. Nora Vance Mending, she wrote on the tag, plainly, because she had not thought of anything better and did not want to oversell it. The first three pieces sold within a week. She gave notice to two of her cleaning houses, keeping only Mrs. Calder's out of stubbornness and a strange new fondness, and told Ferraro she would still take his overflow but could not promise Tuesdays anymore. That evening she took Mia to dinner at the diner they used to visit before everything fell apart, and let her order dessert without checking the price first, watching her daughter's face with a feeling she had not let herself feel in a long time, something close to hope that had started, finally, to seem reasonable.

By autumn, Nora's rack at Priscilla's boutique had grown to take up the whole front window, and a local news blog ran a short piece about the seamstress turning secondhand coats into something new, with a photograph of Nora pinning a hem that Mia had cut out and kept in a shoebox under her bed. Orders came faster than Nora could fill them alone, and she hired a young woman named Talia two afternoons a week to handle the simpler alterations while Nora focused on the rebuilds, which had become, unexpectedly, the part of the work she loved most. She signed a proper lease on a tiny studio above the hardware store, moved the dress form and the thread wall out of the apartment, and stood in the empty room on the day she got the keys, turning in a slow circle, trying to memorize it. She paid off the pawnshop balance on a machine she no longer even needed, just to close that chapter cleanly. Mia, now nine, had started asking to come by after school and thread bobbins at the little side table Nora had set up just for her, and watching her daughter's careful, serious concentration felt like its own kind of payment.

The invitation came on heavy cardstock: a regional design showcase downtown wanted three pieces from Nora Vance Mending for its spring exhibition, alongside designers who had trained at schools Nora had never set foot in. She said yes before she had finished reading the letter twice, then spent six weeks working nights on a coat she considered the best thing she had ever built, its lining printed with a pattern Mia had drawn at the kitchen table one rainy afternoon. On the night of the show, Nora stood at the edge of the room in a dress she had made for herself, watching strangers stop in front of her coat, read the small card with her name on it, and lean in to look at the stitching along the collar. A buyer from a shop two cities over asked for her card before the night was half over. Priscilla found her near the drinks table and hugged her hard enough to lift her slightly off the floor, laughing, saying she had always known, which was not quite true but was kind of her to say. Nora excused herself once, found a quiet hallway, and let herself cry for exactly one minute, the good kind of crying, before fixing her face and going back in.

A year to the day after the factory notice went up on the corkboard, Nora stood in the doorway of her own shop, an actual storefront now, with her name painted in gold on the glass, and watched Mia arrange spools of thread in the front window by color, the way her mother had once done on a single shelf in their old kitchen. Talia and a second employee were fitting a bride's mother for an alteration in the back room, and a rack of reworked coats waited by the door for a delivery to Priscilla's boutique across town. Nora had, that morning, paid off the last of the old debts from the year the machines went quiet, and had cried a little over the receipt before folding it into a drawer she planned never to open again. That evening she took Mia, now ten, to the diner, and this time neither of them thought twice about dessert or the bill or anything at all beyond the plain, sturdy happiness of the day. Walking home past the shop window, its light still glowing over the gold letters of her name, Nora thought that she had spent a year learning to mend things, and had somehow, without quite noticing, mended her own life along the way.

stories.title: Salvage Rights
passages: The distress ping from the Halloway hauler cut out fourteen seconds after it started, and Wren was the one monitoring the boards when it happened. She was sixteen, working her first solo shift in the comms closet of Rockfall Station, half-asleep over a cup of recycled coffee, when the ship her mother and father had taken out to strip a dead freighter simply stopped answering. Rescue skiffs found the wreckage eleven hours later, scattered across two kilometers of vacuum, and there was nothing in it large enough to bring home. Wren stood in the observation bay while the station's chaplain explained, in the gentle administrative voice reserved for these announcements, that a fuel-cell rupture had been logged as the likely cause and that her parents' claim license would revert to the station cooperative within thirty days. She did not cry in front of him. She waited until she was back in the family's cramped berth, surrounded by her father's spare tools and her mother's star charts pinned crookedly to the wall, before the sound came out of her, low and animal, nothing like a word at all. The berth still smelled like both of them. She did not sleep that night, or the next.

The cooperative gave Wren thirty days' grace before the berth reverted too, and by the twenty-eighth day she had sold everything that was not bolted down except her mother's star charts, which she could not make herself part with even when the buyer offered enough credit for two more weeks of food. She moved down to the underdecks, into a shared bunk-stack with people who coughed through the recycled air all night, and learned quickly that being a minor with a dead claim license and an inherited debt for her parents' last unpaid fuel run made her invisible to anyone who might have helped and highly visible to anyone looking to collect. A broker named Tull found her twice in one week to remind her what she owed. She ate from the ration dispenser in the lowest corridor, where the portions were smallest and the credit stretched furthest, and stopped going up to the observation bay at all, because the view of the stars her mother had loved now felt like something aimed directly at her chest. She was sixteen, alone, and could not remember, some days, why getting up mattered more than not.

Wren got taken on by a salvage foreman named Bask who needed a small body that could fit through torn hull sections other crew could not manage, and told herself the work was temporary even after the first month became the third. The suits Bask issued were patched and a size too large, and Wren learned to move through wreckage with her joints locked at odd angles so the loose fabric would not snag on exposed conduit. The pay was calculated by the kilogram of scrap she hauled back, minus the suit rental, minus the oxygen surcharge, minus whatever Bask decided the trip had cost him that week. She came back from every shift with new bruises she did not remember earning and a fine layer of metal dust worked into the creases of her hands that no amount of scrubbing fully removed. She used part of her first real payout to buy back her mother's star charts from the woman who had bought them, paying nearly double what she had received, and did not regret it even as it left her short on food again. Bask called her a fast learner, which was the only compliment anyone had given her in months, and she held onto it harder than it probably deserved.

A hull section collapsed on Wren's fourth month with Bask's crew, pinning her leg against a support strut for eleven minutes while her suit's oxygen reserve ticked down and her crewmates cut through debris that was not supposed to still hold tension. She kept talking on the comm the whole time, mostly to hear a voice, mostly her own, until Bask's second pulled her free with a hydraulic spreader borrowed from a rival crew at a rate that came out of Wren's next four paychecks. The leg was not broken, the medic said, just badly bruised through to the bone, and she would be fine to work again in a week, which meant she went back in four days because a week's wages were a week's wages. She limped through every shift after that, favoring the leg in a way that slowed her down and cost her efficiency bonus, and started to understand, in a way she had not quite let herself before, that this life could kill her the same way it had killed her parents, slowly grinding her down or all at once, and that no one on the station would particularly notice which.

The broker Tull resurfaced once Wren's name started appearing on Bask's manifest sheets, informing her that her parents' fuel debt had accrued interest the cooperative had not mentioned, and that her wages would be garnished directly until it cleared, a timeline he quoted as eleven more years without blinking. Wren argued the math in front of two witnesses at the ration counter and lost, because the cooperative's ledger was the cooperative's ledger and a sixteen-year-old salvager had no standing to dispute it. Her bunk-stack was condemned the same week for a life-support fault the landlord had no intention of fixing, and she spent three nights sleeping in Bask's equipment locker before finding a corner in a worse stack two levels down, damper and colder, shared with twice as many people. She stopped buying anything beyond ration minimums and suit repairs. She still had the star charts, rolled tight and kept against her body inside her jacket, and some nights that felt like the only thing keeping her from becoming exactly the kind of hollowed-out, uncomplaining worker the station seemed built to produce.

An independent captain named Iris Odu hired Wren away from Bask's crew after watching her navigate a debris field the rest of the team had refused to enter, offering a flat wage instead of the per-kilogram scramble and, more importantly, honoring it exactly on schedule. The work was still salvage, still cramped suits and torn hulls, but Iris ran a tight, orderly ship, logged every hour correctly, and split hazard pay evenly rather than skimming it. Wren moved into a proper if narrow cabin aboard Iris's vessel, the Halfway Home, with a door that locked and air that did not taste faintly of mildew. She paid down Tull's interest at a pace that made the eleven-year timeline look more like four, which was not freedom exactly but was at least a number she could imagine reaching. She ate two meals most days instead of one and a half. Nothing about the routine excited her, long runs, methodical stripping of dead vessels, quiet nights doing inventory, but nothing frightened her either, and for the first time since the distress ping had cut out, Wren found she could fall asleep without rehearsing every way the day might have gone wrong.

Iris started teaching Wren the parts of salvage work that went beyond hauling: how to read a derelict's power signature before boarding it, how to tell a dormant reactor from a dead one, how to price a find before a broker could lowball it. Wren was a slow, careful student, which Iris said was better than a fast careless one, and Wren kept a datapad of notes she reviewed before sleep the way her mother used to review star charts. There were setbacks: a run that yielded almost nothing after two days of work, a torn glove that let vacuum-cold bite into her fingers before she sealed it, a week where Tull's office claimed a shipping error and briefly doubled her deduction before Iris got it corrected. But there were small gains too, a bonus for spotting a valuable capacitor array the rest of the crew had walked past, a growing callus of competence replacing the old constant fear. She still kept the star charts against her ribs. She had started, some nights, taking them out and actually looking at them again, rather than simply carrying them.

Iris's sensors picked up an old distress beacon on a routine run through a debris field the charts marked as picked clean decades ago, its signal so faint and strange that two other crews had logged it and moved on without investigating. Wren asked to take the shuttle out to it herself, and Iris, after a long pause, agreed on the condition that Wren report in every ten minutes without fail. The derelict turned out to be older than anything Wren had salvaged before, its hull design unfamiliar, its power core reading as neither dead nor quite alive, something in between that made her instruments flicker uncertainly. She drifted alongside it for a long moment before cutting her own engine, aware that whatever was inside could be worthless corrosion or could be the kind of find that changed a salvager's whole year, and that she would not know which until she was already committed to going in. She thought, briefly and without meaning to, of her mother's hand steadying hers on a similar threshold years ago. Then she radioed Iris her position, checked her tether twice, and cut into the hull.

What Wren found inside was a sealed cargo bay of pre-collapse alloy plating, untouched and uncorroded, the kind of material that had not been manufactured in over a century and that shipwrights across three systems would pay well above scrap rate to get their hands on. She and Iris spent four careful days extracting it without damaging the plates, and the buyer Iris found for it, a restoration yard two jumps out, paid enough that Wren's share alone cleared the remainder of her debt to Tull in a single transfer, with enough left over that she sat holding the confirmation notice for a full minute before she trusted it was real. Word moved fast through the station's close channels: the Halloway girl had found the Century Wreck, as people started calling it, and Bask, of all people, stopped her in the corridor to say he had always known she had an eye for it, which she accepted without correcting the history much. She bought her mother's star charts a proper frame that week, the first thing she had purchased in years that was not strictly necessary, and hung it in her cabin where she would see it every morning.

With the debt cleared and a reputation now attached to her name, Wren used her share of the Century Wreck to lease a small salvage vessel of her own, a battered but sound short-hauler she named the Constance, after her mother. Iris helped her hire a two-person crew, both younger salvagers Wren recognized from her own days in Bask's patched, oversized suits, and she made sure their contracts were flat-rate and paid on schedule, the way Iris had once done for her. The work was harder in some ways, now that the decisions and the risks were hers to carry, but it no longer felt like something happening to her; it felt like something she was building. She took meetings with restoration buyers who addressed her by name and by reputation rather than by suspicion. She sent a portion of every job to the station's dependent fund, quietly, for other salvager kids who might end up where she had started. Bask's old crew occasionally asked her for work now instead of the reverse, and Wren found she did not feel triumphant about that so much as simply, steadily, glad.

When Rockfall Station's main reactor coolant line fractured during a supply lull, with no replacement part closer than three weeks out, it was Wren who remembered the Century Wreck's alloy plating could be machined into a functional seal, and the Constance's small crew who volunteered to fly the emergency retrofit run while station engineers argued over slower alternatives. Wren worked the extraction herself, hands steady despite the whole station's air recyclers ticking down behind her, and delivered the finished component six hours before the backup systems would have failed entirely. The station council called it the fastest emergency salvage fabrication in Rockfall's recorded history, and for one strange, overwhelming evening, people Wren had never spoken to stopped her in the corridors to shake her hand or simply say her name like it meant something good. Iris hugged her outside the council chamber, unembarrassed, and Bask sent over a bottle of something he had clearly been saving for an occasion. Wren stood afterward in the observation bay she had avoided for years after her parents died, looking out at the same stars, and found that the sight no longer felt like something aimed at her chest. It felt, for the first time in a long while, like coming home.

The station council voted, two months later, to rename the observation bay the Halloway Gallery, with a small plaque crediting both the salvager who had saved Rockfall's reactor and the two salvagers, lost years earlier, whose skills had somehow found their way down to her. Wren stood beneath the new plaque at the small ceremony with Iris on one side and her own two crewmates on the other, the framed star charts from her cabin brought along for the occasion and set on a table near the viewport where her mother's careful handwriting caught the starlight. The Constance had three jobs booked for the following month, more than the crew could easily manage, and Wren had already started interviewing a fourth hire, a nervous fifteen-year-old who reminded her, uncomfortably and then warmly, of herself. After the ceremony, she stayed behind alone for a while, running her thumb along the edge of the plaque the way she used to run it along her mother's star charts, and let herself simply feel glad, without bracing for whatever might come to take it away. Outside the viewport, Rockfall's belt turned on, indifferent and vast, and for once that felt like comfort rather than warning.
